ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethical approval was granted by the VU Scientific and Ethical Review Board (reference number 2020.088) and the trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (ID NCT05596396).

Results: Participants were moderately satisfied with the intervention and guidance, and showed small-to-moderate improvements in mental well-being, depressive and anxiety symptoms, and quality of life from baseline to post-intervention (all p < .001; Cohen's d ranging 0.24-0.41).
table.formatted: Results: Participants were moderately satisfied with the intervention and guidance, and showed small-to-moderate improvements in mental well-being, depressive and anxiety symptoms, and quality of life from baseline to post-intervention (all p < .001; Cohen's d ranging 0.24-0.41).

table.text: Participants were recruited through several channels.

The inclusion criteria were as follows: participants had to 1) be aged 16 years or older, 2) be currently enrolled as a student or PhD candidate at a university within the Caring University Consortium, 3) report no active suicidal ideation, and 4) provide informed consent.
Suicidal ideation was measured by asking whether the participant had considered or made plans to end their life.
If answered 'yes', participants were asked how likely they were to act on these plans.
Each time a participant completed a lesson, they would receive a written message from their e-coach regarding that lesson.
Participants had to go through the categories in a fixed order, which can be seen in Table 1 (i.e. from top to bottom).
table.formatted: Participants had to go through the categories in a fixed order, which can be seen in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> (i.e. from top to bottom).

table.text: In this condition, autonomy was limited as participants were not allowed to choose which lessons they wanted to complete and in which order.
In the second version of LifeHack, referred to as the 'autonomy' condition, participants had full autonomy over topic-choice.
Participants were randomly allocated to either the structured or autonomy condition.
All participants that were randomized were included in the primary analyses in accordance with the Intent-to-Treat principle (ITT).
A total of 910 participants were assessed for eligibility between November 2021 and October 2023.

575 participants were randomised and make up our total sample of which 286 participants were randomized to the 'structure' condition and 289 to the 'autonomy' condition A participant flow diagram can be seen in Figure 1.
table.formatted: 575 participants were randomised and make up our total sample of which 286 participants were randomized to the 'structure' condition and 289 to the 'autonomy' condition A participant flow diagram can be seen in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

table.text: The average age of the total sample (n = 575) was 22.6 (SD = 4.33) and most participants were female (80.7%).
Most participants were single (61.7%) and were currently not receiving psychotherapy or medication (83.1%).
In the structured condition (n=286), participants completed an average of 2.36 lessons (SD = 3.13), with a median of 1.
In the autonomy condition (n=289), participants completed an average of 2.21 lessons (SD = 3.29), with a median of 1.

Though participants completed slightly more lessons in the structured condition than the autonomy condition, this difference was not significant: structured condition (n = 286, M = 2.36, SD = 3.13) vs. the autonomy condition (n = 289, M = 2.21, SD = 3.29): t(573)=.569, p=.569.

However, our participants improved from pre-to post-test, and while we did not have an inactive control, our findings may be an indication that even a relatively low adherence can still yield beneficial effects and is therefore acceptable.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: We could find no literature on the effect of autonomy on treatment satisfaction, nor research that directly compares interventions that promote autonomy with those that don't. Therefore, we based our power calculation on a two-tailed difference between means with an effect size of .3 (Cohen, 2013) which is small-to-moderate but still clinically meaningful. Our analysis indicated a total sample size of 580 (290 per arm) (Faul et al., 2007).

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. Participants were recruited through several channels.

The inclusion criteria were as follows: participants had to 1) be aged 16 years or older, 2) be currently enrolled as a student or PhD candidate at a university within the Caring University Consortium, 3) report no active suicidal ideation, and 4) provide informed consent.
Suicidal ideation was measured by asking whether the participant had considered or made plans to end their life.
If answered 'yes', participants were asked how likely they were to act on these plans.
Each time a participant completed a lesson, they would receive a written message from their e-coach regarding that lesson.
Participants had to go through the categories in a fixed order, which can be seen in Table 1 (i.e. from top to bottom).
In this condition, autonomy was limited as participants were not allowed to choose which lessons they wanted to complete and in which order.
In the second version of LifeHack, referred to as the 'autonomy' condition, participants had full autonomy over topic-choice.
Participants were randomly allocated to either the structured or autonomy condition.
All participants that were randomized were included in the primary analyses in accordance with the Intent-to-Treat principle (ITT).
A total of 910 participants were assessed for eligibility between November 2021 and October 2023.

575 participants were randomised and make up our total sample of which 286 participants were randomized to the 'structure' condition and 289 to the 'autonomy' condition A participant flow diagram can be seen in Figure 1.
The average age of the total sample (n = 575) was 22.6 (SD = 4.33) and most participants were female (80.7%).
Most participants were single (61.7%) and were currently not receiving psychotherapy or medication (83.1%).
In the structured condition (n=286), participants completed an average of 2.36 lessons (SD = 3.13), with a median of 1.
In the autonomy condition (n=289), participants completed an average of 2.21 lessons (SD = 3.29), with a median of 1.

Though participants completed slightly more lessons in the structured condition than the autonomy condition, this difference was not significant: structured condition (n = 286, M = 2.36, SD = 3.13) vs. the autonomy condition (n = 289, M = 2.21, SD = 3.29): t(573)=.569, p=.569.

However, our participants improved from pre-to post-test, and while we did not have an inactive control, our findings may be an indication that even a relatively low adherence can still yield beneficial effects and is therefore acceptable.

text.text: Background: College students face high rates of mental health problems including depression and stress.
Digital interventions offer accessible support, but adherence remains challenging.
Autonomy may enhance motivation, yet its role in studentfocused digital interventions is not explored yet in a randomized controlled trial.

Objective: This study examines whether enhancing autonomy in a guided digital CBT-based mental health intervention for college students (LifeHack) improves satisfaction, adherence, and mental health outcomes.
Methods: In a two-armed randomized trial, 575 students were assigned to either a structured intervention or an autonomy-enhanced version in which participants could select topics of interest.
Assessments were conducted at baseline and 5 weeks later (post-intervention).

Primary outcomes were general satisfaction (CSQ-8) and working alliance with the program and e-coach (WAI-I); secondary outcomes included adherence, mental well-being (MHC-SF), depressive symptoms (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), and quality of life (MHQoL).

Results: Participants were moderately satisfied with the intervention and guidance, and showed small-to-moderate improvements in mental well-being, depressive and anxiety symptoms, and quality of life from baseline to post-intervention (all p < .001; Cohen's d ranging 0.24-0.41).
text.formatted: Results: Participants were moderately satisfied with the intervention and guidance, and showed small-to-moderate improvements in mental well-being, depressive and anxiety symptoms, and quality of life from baseline to post-intervention (all p < .001; Cohen's d ranging 0.24-0.41).

text.text: However, no significant differences were observed between conditions on satisfaction, adherence or clinical outcomes.
Conclusions: Allowing users to freely choose lesson topics did not enhance satisfaction, adherence, or clinical outcomes compared with a structured lesson sequence.
Nonetheless, participation in LifeHack was associated with improved mental health, indicating potential intervention effectiveness regardless of the autonomy features.
Future research should test more comprehensive autonomysupportive designs and compare LifeHack with inactive control conditions to establish intervention effectiveness.

text.text: These high prevalence rates and detrimental consequences make student mental health a significant cause of concern.

text.text: Autonomy, which is the experience of having choice and ownership over one's actions, is widely recognized as a key driver of sustained, self-endorsed behavior (Ryan et al., 2008; Ryan & Deci, 2020).

text.text: Furthermore, interventions that actively support autonomy have demonstrated small but significant positive effects on physical health behavior change, with autonomy functioning as an important mechanism underlying these effects (Ng et al., 2012; Sheeran et al., 2020).

text.text: In the context of mental health, however, the explicit integration of autonomy as a deliberate design element in digital interventions remains relatively underexplored.

Recent reviews of psychotherapy innovations further suggest that, while many digital and therapeutic approaches show promise, no single advancement is expected to dramatically improve outcomes on its own.
Instead, progress in both effectiveness and uptake is likely to result from multiple, incremental improvements across intervention design, delivery, and personalization (Cuijpers et al., 2026).

text.text: In this context, autonomy-enhancing features such as offering participants choices can be considered one such incremental improvement.

In the current study, we developed a new guided digital intervention (LifeHack) for the general college student population aimed at improving their mental health, which includes such an incremental improvement.
In an autonomy-enhanced version, participants can choose the topics they find to be most relevant.
The other version follows a structured format in which topics have to be completed in a predefined order.
To investigate the impact of autonomy, these two version are compared headto-head in a randomized controlled trial.

Our primary outcome is satisfaction, and the secondary outcomes are guidance satisfaction, adherence (number of lessons completed), general mental well-being, depressive symptoms, anxiety, and overall quality of life.
>Methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Methods</head>

text.text: This study was a two-arm randomized trial among college students seeking to improve their mental health, comparing a structured versus an autonomy-enhanced version of a guided e-health intervention (LifeHack).
Assessments were conducted at baseline (T0) and five weeks later (post-intervention (T1).
This study was conducted within the Caring Universities Consortium; a collaboration between several large Dutch colleges.
The Caring Universities Consortium is affiliated with the World Health Organization (WHO) World Mental Health International College Student Initiative (WMH-ICS) (Cuijpers, Auerbach, et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The Caring Universities Consortium is affiliated with the World Health Organization (WHO) World Mental Health International College Student Initiative (WMH-ICS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cuijpers, Auerbach, et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Ethical approval was granted by the VU Scientific and Ethical Review Board (reference number 2020.088) and the trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (ID NCT05596396).
Students enrolled in any of the participating universities were eligible to register for LifeHack.
Participants were recruited through several channels.
First, through oncampus marketing efforts (e.g. posters, flyers) as well as social media posts.
Second, staff members including student psychologists and student mentors were encouraged to refer students to LifeHack.
Lastly, Caring Universities through a yearly WMH-ICS survey sent to all students via email and informating them about LifeHack.
Participant recruitment and data collection took place from November 2021 to October 2023.
No compensation was offered for participation.

The inclusion criteria were as follows: participants had to 1) be aged 16 years or older, 2) be currently enrolled as a student or PhD candidate at a university within the Caring University Consortium, 3) report no active suicidal ideation, and 4) provide informed consent.
Suicidal ideation was measured by asking whether the participant had considered or made plans to end their life.
If answered 'yes', participants were asked how likely they were to act on these plans.
Participants that responded with "somewhat likely" or "very likely" were excluded from the intervention and referred to more appropriate mental healthcare.
LifeHack is a CBT-based online intervention designed to improve the mental health of the general student population.
It consists of 12 lessons which can be categorized into four themes: emotional well-being, studies, social life, self-esteem, along with an introductory and concluding lesson (see Table 1).
text.formatted: It consists of 12 lessons which can be categorized into four themes: emotional well-being, studies, social life, self-esteem, along with an introductory and concluding lesson (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The lesson topics were selected in a two step process: first, clinical psychology experts from the Caring Universities Consortium created a longlist of mental healthrelated topics they considered beneficial for students.
Second, this list was presented to a group of students (n=156) who were asked to identify the most relevant topics.
The topics selected by the most students were incorporated into the program.

Each lesson was developed using cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) as a general framework, while also drawing on principles from positive psychology, behavior change approaches, and interpersonal skills and incorporating student input.
Each lesson contained a mix of psychoeducation, reflective questions, interactive exercises, and homework assignments.
In order to ensure the program was engaging and appealing, we used text as well as visuals in the form of illustrations, infographics and videos.
Each lesson took around 30 minutes to complete.
The intervention could be accessed on any device that had internet connection.
All LifeHack participants received text-based guidance by an e-coach.
The ecoaches were master students Clinical Psychology from the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam who received training by and supervision from a psychologist with ecoaching experience.
During registration, a participant could choose one of three ecoaches based on a photograph and short biography.
Each time a participant completed a lesson, they would receive a written message from their e-coach regarding that lesson.
The coaching process was as follows: an e-coach would read a participant's answers to the reflective questions and assignments in a lesson.

They would then write a coaching message within three working days using motivational interviewing techniques by making affirmations, asking open ended questions, and using reflections (Hall et al., 2012).
text.formatted: They would then write a coaching message within three working days using motivational interviewing techniques by making affirmations, asking open ended questions, and using reflections <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hall et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The e-coach would send this message to the participant via the platform, who would then receive an email notification that a new coach message is available to them upon logging into the intervention.

To examine the effect of the principle of autonomy on intervention adherence, this study compared two versions of LifeHack that contained exactly the same content and guidance, but they differed in the way the content was offered.
In the first version, the 'structured' condition, autonomy was limited.
Participants had to go through the categories in a fixed order, which can be seen in Table 1 (i.e. from top to bottom).

text.text: In this condition, autonomy was limited as participants were not allowed to choose which lessons they wanted to complete and in which order.
In the second version of LifeHack, referred to as the 'autonomy' condition, participants had full autonomy over topic-choice.
They could access all categories and lessons upon completing the introductory lesson.
They could choose which lessons they wanted to complete and which to skip, as well as how many and in which order.
Participants were randomly allocated to either the structured or autonomy condition.
We used 1:1 block randomization via an automated online system built in with the Caring Universities platform, stratified by gender and university.
Conditions were automatically assigned upon completion of the baseline assessment.
This automated procedure ensured that the allocation was blinded.

We assessed the following sociodemographic data: age, gender, marital status, nationality, current university, education level (Bachelor, Master or Ph.D.), and current usage of psychotherapy (yes/no) and/or psychofarmaca (yes/no).
Participant's satisfaction with the intervention was measured using the Client Satisfaction Questionnaire (CSQ-8) (Larsen et al., 1979).

text.text: The CSQ-8 assesses overall satisfaction, including perceived quality and service, usefulness, and whether participants would reuse or recommend the intervention.
It comprises eight items rated on a 4-point Likert scale (sum score 8-32), with higher scores indicating greater satisfaction.

In this study, adherence was measured by calculating how many of the 14 lessons were completed by participants, which was tracked by the digital platform.

Therefore, we based our power calculation on a two-tailed difference between means with an effect size of .3 (Cohen, 2013) which is small-to-moderate but still clinically meaningful.

text.text: IBM SPSS version 30 was used for the statistical analyses.
All participants that were randomized were included in the primary analyses in accordance with the Intent-to-Treat principle (ITT).
First, we examined differences in baseline characteristics between the two study arms (i.e., the structure and autonomy conditions) to assess the success of randomization.
We also compared study completers and non-completers to determine whether attrition may have introduced systematic bias.
These analyses were conducted using chi-square tests and independent-samples t-tests.

For the satisfaction analyses, missing data were handled using multiple imputation with 60 imputed datasets generated via Fully Conditional Specification (FCS) and pooled results were computed using Rubin's rules.
We examined differences between our two arms in satisfaction (CSQ-8, WAI-I) and adherence with independent sample t-tests.
We calculated effect sizes (Cohen's d) manually based on the pooled results and interpreted using the benchmarks of 0.2 (small effect), 0.5 (moderate effect), and 0.8 (large effect) (Cohen, 2013).

text.text: Linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) were used to examine the effects of program version, time, and their interaction on all clinical oucome scores (i.e.
MHC-SF, PHQ-9, GAD-7, MHQoL).

The LLMs were conducted on the original data (i.e. not imputed), consistent with evidence that mixed-model analyses of longitudinal data can validly accommodate missing values without the need for multiple imputation (Twisk et al., 2013).

text.text: We included sociodemographics (age, gender, marital status, nationality, university, education level, psychotherapy and/or medication) and baseline clinical scores as potential covariates in our analyses as these factors have been shown to possibly moderate the effectiveness of interventions (Ebert et al., 2013; Karyotaki et al., 2018; Reins et al., 2020).

text.text: Models were estimated using restricted maximum likelihood (REML).
Estimated marginal means (EMMs) were calculated from the LMM and we examined both time*group as well as time effects.
Effect sizes were calculated manually based on the EMMs.
Lastly, we performed additional sensitivity analyses and repeated all the analyses for two subgroups.
First, we did a Complete Case Analysis (CCA) analyzing only participants with complete data at post-measure.
Second, we analysed only participants that had completed at least one lesson, and were therefore guaranteed to have been exposed to the autonomy-manipulation.
>Results
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Results</head>

text.text: A total of 910 participants were assessed for eligibility between November 2021 and October 2023.

Of these, 145 dropped during baseline assessment, 152 dropped out during account creation, and 38 were excluded due to active suicidal ideation and referred to other forms of mental health support (GP, psychologist).

575 participants were randomised and make up our total sample of which 286 participants were randomized to the 'structure' condition and 289 to the 'autonomy' condition A participant flow diagram can be seen in Figure 1.

text.text: The average age of the total sample (n = 575) was 22.6 (SD = 4.33) and most participants were female (80.7%).
The majority was from the Netherlands (62.1%) or another European country (29.7%), and were currently in their first bachelor year (32.2%) or master's (37.4%).
Most participants were single (61.7%) and were currently not receiving psychotherapy or medication (83.1%).

On average, participants indicated moderate general mental health (MHC-SF M = 38.04) and quality of life (MHQoL M = 13.21), and had mild levels of depression (PHQ-9 M = 8.33) and anxiety (GAD-7 M = 7.29).
We compared baseline characteristics (i.e. age, gender, nationality, university, education level, marital status, current professional help, PHQ-9, GAD-7, MHC-SF, MHQoL) between the two arms.
Participants in the 'autonomy' condition scored higher on baseline anxiety (M= 7.8) and depression (M= 8.8) compared to the 'structured' condition (M=6.8 and 7.8 respectively).

text.text: Our main analyses were performed on all randomized patients.
We then repeated all analyses on two subgroups of students.
First, a complete case analysis (CCA) including only students who completed post-test measures.
Second, examining participants that completed at least one lesson.
The results for both subgroups were very similar to those of the total sample: there were no significant differences between groups on satisfaction, adherence and mental health outcomes.
Across groups, there was a significant time effect for all mental health outcomes.
>Discussion
text.formatted: <head n="4." >Discussion</head>

text.text: The present trial examined the effects of autonomy in a newly developed, guided digital CBT-based intervention (LifeHack) aimed at improving mental health in college students.
Participants received one of two versions of LifeHack that differed only in the degree of autonomy.

At baseline, participants displayed moderate general mental health problems as well as mild levels of depression and anxiety, although patients in the autonomy condition showed slightly more symptoms than those in the structured condition.
Participants indicated being moderately satisfied with the general intervention as well as with the guidance and there were no statistically significant differences between the two groups.
There were also no significant differences in the number of completed lessons (M=2.3).

Across both conditions, participants showed statistically significant improvements over time in general mental well-being (d=.24), quality of life (d=.41), depressive symptoms (d=.36) and anxiety symptoms (d=.38) but there were no statistically significant differences between the two groups.

Sensitivity analyses using complete-case analyses and only participants that completed at least one lesson yielded patterns consistent with the main results, further strengthening the conclusion that enhancing autonomy by letting participants choose topics of interest within the intervention did not significantly enhance satisfaction, adherence or clinical outcomes in the present study.
The absence of between-group differences did not confirm our hypothesis that increasing autonomy would enhance satisfaction, adherence, and clinical outcomes.

To our knowledge, no studies directly examined the effect of autonomy in digital mental health interventions, however, autonomy was shown to have small positive effects on physical health behavior change (Sheeran et al., 2020).
text.formatted: To our knowledge, no studies directly examined the effect of autonomy in digital mental health interventions, however, autonomy was shown to have small positive effects on physical health behavior change <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Sheeran et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: One possible explanation for our lack of findings regarding autonomy relates to the presentation of the content in the autonomy condition: displaying all 14 topics simultaneously may have increased cognitive load or induced choice paralysis, potentially offsetting the intended benefits of autonomy (Iyengar & Lepper, 2000).
text.formatted: One possible explanation for our lack of findings regarding autonomy relates to the presentation of the content in the autonomy condition: displaying all 14 topics simultaneously may have increased cognitive load or induced choice paralysis, potentially offsetting the intended benefits of autonomy <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Iyengar & Lepper, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, common elements across conditions (e.g., content and guidance) may have overshadowed any incremental benefit of autonomy.
Our findings should be interpreted in light of recent work emphasizing that revolutionary progress in digital mental health is unlikely to result from single, isolated innovations.
Instead, improvements are expected from the accumulation of incremental refinements in intervention design and delivery (Cuijpers et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Instead, improvements are expected from the accumulation of incremental refinements in intervention design and delivery <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Cuijpers et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The autonomy manipulation in the present study can be viewed as one such incremental refinement.
While theoretically grounded and practically relevant, the manipulation may have been insufficient to produce measurable effects.

Our findings therefore do not undermine the relevance of autonomy as a motivational principle, but rather highlight the challenge of detecting small, additive effects in real-world digital interventions.
Participant satisfaction in the present study was in line with prior digital intervention research.

Studies on interventions across a range of mental health complaints (i.e. stress, depression, procrastination) for college students report moderate to high satisfaction rates (Ozmen et al., 2025; Rahmadiana et al., 2021; Terp et al., 2022).

text.text: This further strengthens the notion that digital interventions are generally acceptable to college students.

While adherence rates were in line with findings from similar open-access online mental health interventions offered within the Caring Universities Consortium (Amanvermez et al., 2023; Ozmen et al., 2025), they were on the lower side when compared with other student mental health interventions (Harrer et al., 2018; Palacios et al., 2018; Rith-Najarian et al., 2024).
text.formatted: While adherence rates were in line with findings from similar open-access online mental health interventions offered within the Caring Universities Consortium <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Amanvermez et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Ozmen et al., 2025)</ref>, they were on the lower side when compared with other student mental health interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Harrer et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Palacios et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Rith-Najarian et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, these latter studies either offered financial compensation for study participation, only included participants with elevated clinical symptoms who may have been more motivated to engage with the treatment, or used automated daily motivational SMS reminders.
The present study was for the general student population who averaged only mild levels of depression and anxiety, and we offered no compensation nor phone-based reminders.
These differences likely contributed to the comparatively lower adherence observed in our study.

However, our participants improved from pre-to post-test, and while we did not have an inactive control, our findings may be an indication that even a relatively low adherence can still yield beneficial effects and is therefore acceptable.

Consistent with meta-analyses showing that (digital) mental health interventions can effectively improve outcomes in students (Cuijpers et al., 2021), the present study found that participants from both versions of LifeHack showed small to moderate improvements in well-being, depression, anxiety, and quality of life from pre-to posttest, though we cannot directly attribute these to the intervention due to the lack of an inactive control group.

text.text: The present study has several limitations.
The first limitation concerns the operationalization of the construct of 'autonomy'.
Autonomy was implemented as the ability to choose intervention topics, which may represent a relatively narrow manipulation of the construct.
The intervention may have benefited from additional autonomy-enhancing features such as goal-setting, task options and feedback options (Alberts et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The intervention may have benefited from additional autonomy-enhancing features such as goal-setting, task options and feedback options <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Alberts et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, presenting all topics simultaneously may have increased cognitive load or choice paralysis (Iyengar & Lepper, 2000), potentially reducing engagement.
text.formatted: Additionally, presenting all topics simultaneously may have increased cognitive load or choice paralysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Iyengar & Lepper, 2000)</ref>, potentially reducing engagement.

text.text: Consequently, the autonomy manipulation in the present study may not have been sufficiently impactful to produce measurable effects.
A second limitation is the high attrition rate (37.7% completion).
High attrition can introduce bias when participants who discontinue differ systematically from those who complete the study, potentially affecting the validity of the findings (Nunan et al., 2018).
text.formatted: High attrition can introduce bias when participants who discontinue differ systematically from those who complete the study, potentially affecting the validity of the findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Nunan et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The observed attrition may partly reflect characteristics of the study design: the intervention was implemented in a naturalistic setting and offered as a service for students, and participants may not have been highly motivated to complete assessments.

While this low-threshold and scalable design increases ecological validity and accessibility, it may also reduce engagement with the assessments, contributing to higher attrition and potential attrition bias.
However, no meaningful differences were observed between study completers and non-completers, suggesting that the risk of attrition bias may be limited.
A key strength of the present study is its novel theoretical contribution.
We experimentally isolated a single autonomy-supportive design element and compared two otherwise identical interventions that differed only in this element.

Although autonomy is widely recognized as an important factor in physical health behavior change (Sheeran et al., 2020), to our knowledge, prior research has not directly tested the effect of a clearly defined autonomy-supportive component within a controlled design.
text.formatted: Although autonomy is widely recognized as an important factor in physical health behavior change <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Sheeran et al., 2020)</ref>, to our knowledge, prior research has not directly tested the effect of a clearly defined autonomy-supportive component within a controlled design.

text.text: The present study contributes to a still limited body of research examining the specific mechanisms that foster motivation and enhance the effectiveness of digital interventions.
Another notable strength is the ecological validity of the study.
The present intervention was delivered as part of a large-scale mental health platform available to college students across the Netherlands, rather than under highly controlled trial conditions.
This real-life implementation ensures the generalizability of our findings to similar large-scale, routine care settings (Glasgow et al., 1999).
text.formatted: This real-life implementation ensures the generalizability of our findings to similar large-scale, routine care settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Glasgow et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: It also suggests the potential feasibility of integrating mental health interventions within the infrastructure of higher education, indicating that such approaches may have the capacity for wide-reaching impact in student populations (Andersson & Titov, 2014; Ebert et al., 2018).

text.text: Given the increasing mental health needs among college students (Auerbach et al., 2018), the ability to implement and evaluate interventions for students is both timely and critical.

text.text: We have several recommendations for future research.
First, the optimization of the autonomy-supportive intervention.

To improve the process of topic selection, we recommend incorporating a tool into LifeHack to help participants identify the most relevant topic(s) to their current needs rather than presenting all 14 at once and potentially creating clutter and mental overload.
Such a tool could analyse a participant's baseline assessment data and make a suggestion for most relevant topic.
In addition, participants could read a one-sentence description of each lesson to select the most relevant one(s), which would then become the focus of the intervention.

To further support autonomy, we recommend incorporating a brief goalsetting exercise within each lesson, allowing participants to identify specific goals and reflect on their personal reasons for change (Alberts et al., 2024).
text.formatted: To further support autonomy, we recommend incorporating a brief goalsetting exercise within each lesson, allowing participants to identify specific goals and reflect on their personal reasons for change <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Alberts et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Lastly, participants could be offered meaningful choices in how they complete exercises (e.g., a writing reflection or a guided audio exercise), enabling them to select the format that best fits their preferences or context (Alberts et al., 2024).

text.text: A second recommendation for future research is to evaluate LifeHack's effectiveness as a mental health intervention for students.
Although this study primarily examined the role of autonomy, participants did show significant improvements across outcomes in both conditions.

However, the absence of an inactive control group prevents causal attribution of these improvements to the intervention, as alternative explanations such as regression to the mean or spontaneous recovery cannot be ruled out (Mohr et al., 2009).
text.formatted: However, the absence of an inactive control group prevents causal attribution of these improvements to the intervention, as alternative explanations such as regression to the mean or spontaneous recovery cannot be ruled out <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Mohr et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should therefore employ a randomized controlled design with a wait-list or no-treatment condition to establish the intervention's effectiveness.

The present trial did not find evidence that adding a single autonomy-supportive feature to a guided digital mental health intervention for students improved satisfaction, adherence, or clinical outcomes.

These findings suggest that introducing a single autonomy design element such as allowing participants to choose lesson topics may be insufficient to produce measurable improvements in engagement or outcomes.
Rather, meaningful gains in digital mental health interventions may require the cumulative effect of multiple design features.

Nonetheless, this study represents an important initial step in applying autonomy within digital mental health interventions, offering valid insights from a real-world university setting and offering clear directions for future intervention development and research.
